paragraphs: A medical image can be analyzed by assigning a label to the whole image or by identifying the regions associated with a finding. Classification has historically been cheaper to label, but reduced costs for training segmentation models motivate this paper to revisit that choice. The authors ask how these two formulations affect performance on the same underlying task.

They first use information theory to examine why classification and segmentation can learn differently from the same dataset. They then implement several ways of using segmentation outputs to classify medical images and compare these approaches with conventional classification on three retrospective datasets. This connects the conceptual analysis to practical alternatives for producing image-level decisions.

Reported benefits include learning with up to an order of magnitude fewer labeled images, improved performance for low-prevalence classes, and up to 161.1% improved recall for certain rare subgroups. The abstract also reports up to 44.8% improved robust AUROC against spurious correlations, alongside better interpretability and error analysis. These are reported advantages in the studied settings, with the largest gains describing particular cases.
neurips-2023-a-case-for-reframing-automa.tldr: The paper examines using segmentation to classify medical images and reports gains in sample efficiency, robustness, and interpretability across three retrospective datasets.

paragraphs: Many scientific datasets come with transformations that a predictive model should respect. An equivariant network preserves the relationship between transforming its input and transforming its output. This paper develops a general architecture for symmetries described by finite-dimensional representations of reductive Lie groups, a family that includes orthogonal, Lorentz, and unitary groups.

The approach extends the ACE and MACE architectures beyond their atomistic point-cloud setting. Its scope is data that transforms according to an action of a reductive Lie group. The authors also introduce lie-nn, a software library supporting construction of these networks. A central capability decomposes tensor products of representations into irreducible representations, providing mathematical building blocks for implementing the architecture across different groups.

The authors demonstrate the framework on top quark decay tagging using Lorentz symmetry and shape recognition using orthogonal symmetry. These applications illustrate how one architectural framework can accommodate distinct transformation rules. The contribution combines a broad symmetry-respecting construction with implementation tools and demonstrations in two different problem settings.
neurips-2023-a-general-framework-for-equ.tldr: A general architecture and supporting library extend equivariant neural networks to finite-dimensional representations of any reductive Lie group.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must choose actions using a fixed collection of past experience. When that collection explores only a limited part of the environment, a learned policy can encounter situations poorly represented in its training data. This paper addresses the resulting distribution mismatch through a two-level interaction between policy learning and value estimation.

The lower level constructs a confidence set of value estimates. These estimates must have sufficiently small weighted average Bellman errors while accounting for uncertainty caused by distribution mismatch. The upper level then chooses a policy by maximizing a conservative value from that set. A penalized adversarial estimation procedure makes this formulation computationally practical while preserving flexibility in the exploratory distribution it implicitly uses.

The theoretical regret guarantees require realizability but do not require data-coverage or completeness assumptions. Within the proposed theoretical setting, the authors characterize the learned policy as a best-effort solution among the available policies. Experiments spanning synthetic, benchmark, and real-world datasets show competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods, connecting the theoretical formulation with practical offline learning.
neurips-2023-bi-level-offline-policy-opt.tldr: A two-level offline reinforcement learning method optimizes conservative value estimates and provides regret guarantees requiring realizability without coverage or completeness assumptions.

paragraphs: Encoder APIs turn inputs into vector representations that users can reuse for machine learning tasks. Because the underlying encoders are expensive to train, an attacker may collect API outputs to build a cheaper local copy. Bucks for Buckets, or B4B, introduces an active defense that changes what the API returns while a stealing attempt is underway.

The defense rests on an observed difference in usage. Attackers trying to reproduce broad encoder functionality cover substantially more of the embedding space than legitimate users solving a particular downstream task. B4B tracks that coverage and adaptively adjusts the usefulness of returned representations. The authors present this as a way to interfere with stealing while preserving representation quality for legitimate use.

B4B also addresses attackers who spread queries across multiple accounts. It applies a different transformation to each user's representations, preventing straightforward pooling of outputs from those accounts into one training collection. Together, coverage-sensitive responses and account-specific transformations target both broad collection and direct cross-account aggregation, making the API itself part of the proposed defense.
neurips-2023-bucks-for-buckets-b4b-activ.tldr: B4B actively defends encoder APIs by adjusting outputs according to embedding-space coverage and transforming representations separately for each user.

paragraphs: Tracking Any Point asks a model to follow selected image points through a video and recover their long-term trajectories. Earlier approaches estimated trajectories independently to accommodate longer image sequences. This paper argues that such independent tracking can still benefit from spatial context: the visual information surrounding a point can help determine where it moves.

Context-PIPs adds a framework for collecting and using that context. It has two main components, Source Feature Enhancement and Target Feature Aggregation. These modules bring spatial context into the features used for trajectory estimation. The central contribution is to improve independent point tracking through richer visual representations, preserving the focus on individual trajectories while drawing information from their surroundings.

The reported results show improvements over PIPs on two video benchmarks. On CroHD, the average trajectory error for occluded points falls by 11.4%. On TAP-Vid-Kinetics, the average percentage of correct keypoints increases by 11.8%. These findings support the paper's argument that spatial context can improve trajectory accuracy, including when points are hidden from view.
neurips-2023-context-pips-persistent-ind.tldr: Context-PIPs improves long-term video point tracking by enhancing source features and aggregating target features with spatial context.

paragraphs: Learning depth from unlabeled monocular video becomes difficult when objects move independently. A change in an object's image position can be explained by its motion or by a different estimated depth. Methods that assume a static scene can therefore assign incorrect depths to moving objects, even when their explanation of the visible movement appears plausible.

Dynamo-Depth tackles this ambiguity by jointly learning three quantities: monocular depth, a three-dimensional field describing independent motion, and a segmentation of motion. Its key insight concerns initialization. The authors state that a sufficiently good initial motion segmentation is enough to support joint learning of depth and independent motion despite the underlying ambiguity. This is a sufficient condition, rather than a claim that the ambiguity disappears for every initialization.

The method learns from unlabeled monocular videos and reports state-of-the-art depth estimation on Waymo Open and nuScenes. The abstract highlights substantial improvement in estimated depth for moving objects. These results connect the proposed handling of motion ambiguity to the cases where static-scene training assumptions are particularly problematic.
neurips-2023-dynamo-depth-fixing-unsuper.tldr: Dynamo-Depth jointly learns depth, independent motion, and motion segmentation, using good initial segmentation to resolve ambiguity around moving objects.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks combine graph connections with node features through message passing. Computing the full product of an adjacency matrix and a feature matrix can be expensive on large graphs. This paper studies whether much of that work can be avoided in a specific setting: regression with a two-layer linear graph convolutional network.

The algorithm first subsamples nodes, then uses the smaller graph to estimate leverage scores for the full adjacency-feature product. Those scores guide a further sampling step. This arrangement aims to identify informative parts of the computation without first constructing the entire product whose cost the method is trying to avoid.

For n nodes, d features, and accuracy parameter ε, the method observes O(nd ε⁻² log n) adjacency entries and takes O(nd² ε⁻² log n) time. The learned weights are guaranteed to be within ε in Euclidean norm of those obtained using the full adjacency matrix. Experiments on real-world graph regression problems outperform alternative sampling strategies given the same observation budget. The guarantee concerns this linear regression setting and closeness of learned weights.
neurips-2023-efficient-learning-of-linea.tldr: Node subsampling and estimated leverage scores train a two-layer linear graph model efficiently while bounding its weight difference from full-graph training.

paragraphs: An embodied agent must act on what it sees, so environmental or physical changes can alter the observations on which its policy depends. This paper addresses efficient policy learning and adaptation to such changes. Its Contrastive Prompt Ensemble framework, ConPE, combines a pretrained vision-language model with multiple learned visual prompts to construct more robust state representations.

Each prompt is trained contrastively around an individual domain factor that affects the agent's first-person observations. A guided attention mechanism combines the prompts. For a particular task, the attention-based ensemble and the policy are learned together, allowing the representation to reflect both variation across domains and information useful for choosing task-relevant actions.

Experiments cover navigation in AI2THOR, manipulation in Metaworld, and autonomous driving in CARLA. The authors report that ConPE outperforms other state-of-the-art algorithms in these settings while improving the sample efficiency of policy learning and adaptation. The findings support combining factor-focused prompts with task-specific attention as a practical route toward adaptation across changing visual conditions.
neurips-2023-efficient-policy-adaptation.tldr: ConPE combines contrastively learned visual prompts through task-trained attention to improve embodied agents' policy performance and adaptation efficiency.

paragraphs: Datasets for computer vision involving people shape how systems are evaluated for fairness and reliability. This paper examines curation practices that neglect privacy and bias, including nonconsensual web scraping. Such collections can lack the contextual metadata needed for thorough fairness and robustness evaluations, while problematic practices have contributed to dataset withdrawals and unfair models.

The authors develop proactive recommendations specifically for human-centric computer vision evaluation datasets. Their considerations cover the dataset's purpose, privacy and consent, and diversity. The approach asks curators to reflect on these issues before constructing a dataset, drawing on existing practices, guidelines, withdrawals, and audits to inform the recommendations.

The paper also explains why current remedies can be inadequate: they may arrive after problems emerge, offer weak reasons for adoption, or omit context needed to determine appropriate use. Its contribution is a domain-specific framework for earlier reflection. This positions responsible curation as part of designing a meaningful evaluation resource, with purpose and collection practices considered alongside the data's suitability for assessing models.
neurips-2023-ethical-considerations-for-.tldr: The paper develops proactive recommendations on purpose, consent, privacy, and diversity for curating human-centric computer vision evaluation datasets.

paragraphs: Dynamic Sparse Training trains a neural network while repeatedly changing which connections are active. It starts with sparse connectivity and alternates between removing weights and growing connections elsewhere. Under particular conditions, this approach has been shown to outperform dense models. Its behavior therefore depends on both how new connections are selected and how existing ones are removed.

This paper focuses on the removal step, which has received less attention than connection growth. The authors conduct an extensive empirical comparison of pruning criteria to study how they affect the dynamics and outcomes of sparse training. The question is whether more elaborate rules for deciding which weights to discard produce meaningful improvements.

Most of the investigated criteria give similar results. Differences become more pronounced when very few connections remain active, and simple magnitude-based pruning predominantly delivers the best performance in that low-density regime. This finding gives practical weight to a straightforward criterion. It remains an empirical conclusion about the studied methods and settings, rather than a universal ranking of every possible pruning rule.
neurips-2023-fantastic-weights-and-how-t.tldr: An empirical study finds that pruning criteria often perform similarly in dynamic sparse training, with magnitude pruning predominantly best at low density.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from clients that keep their datasets local. Different client data can produce inconsistent models and updates pointing in nearly orthogonal directions. Combining those updates can shrink the overall update norm and slow convergence. FedMRUR addresses both model inconsistency and the reduced size of the aggregated update.

Its regularizer encourages local and global models to produce nearby data representations in a low-dimensional hyperbolic graph space. The authors argue that this geometry can reflect model bias better than Euclidean distances between parameters or gradients. A separate global optimizer aggregates client update norms to determine the global update norm, mitigating the reduction associated with nearly orthogonal client contributions.

The paper proves a convergence rate of O(1/√(SKT)) in a non-convex setting with partial participation, where S counts participating clients, K is the local interval, and T counts communication rounds. The authors describe this as a linear speedup property. Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy with less communication, supporting the combined use of representation alignment and update rescaling.
neurips-2023-federated-learning-with-man.tldr: FedMRUR aligns client representations in hyperbolic space and rescales aggregated updates to improve federated learning under heterogeneous client data.

paragraphs: Large training collections have helped drive progress in vision and language, but quantum chemistry datasets face an expensive labeling process. Their targets are often calculated using density functional theory, or DFT. This paper addresses that computational bottleneck by introducing PySCF_IPU, a data generator that uses Intelligence Processing Units to accelerate dataset creation.

The resulting QM1B dataset contains one billion training examples with 9–11 heavy atoms. The authors contrast this scale with existing datasets containing roughly 100,000 to 20 million examples and describe accelerator use as a first step beyond earlier CPU-supercomputer-based generation. They also test whether simply providing more data benefits a neural predictor without adding new inductive biases.

Their SchNet 9M baseline improves as the amount of training data increases. This supports the value of scale for the tested model, while the authors explicitly emphasize limitations of QM1B, especially the low resolution of its DFT choices. The dataset therefore demonstrates expanded data generation capacity while motivating future collections that combine greater scale with more accurate labels.
neurips-2023-generating-qm1b-with-pyscf-.tldr: PySCF_IPU enables the billion-example QM1B chemistry dataset, demonstrating benefits from more training data while highlighting low-resolution DFT labels.

paragraphs: Non-convex optimization can produce candidate solutions whose quality is difficult to establish. This paper develops an approach that combines optimization with certificates, providing mathematical support for assessing the result. It applies to smooth functions defined on a hypercube or a torus and seeks to make certified optimization more computationally scalable.

The method uses regularity expressed through the decay of a function's Fourier spectrum. The authors construct a tractable model family that supports precise certificates while allowing use of computational techniques developed for neural network optimization. This connection makes GPU parallelism available to the optimization process, tying the mathematical representation to a practical route for handling larger problems.

The reported comparison concerns polynomials in moderate dimensions with thousands of coefficients. In that setting, the approach outperforms state-of-the-art certified optimization methods, including methods based on Lasserre's hierarchy, and handles problems that competitors find intractable. The significance is a demonstrated expansion of tractable certified optimization in this regime, supported by a method designed around smoothness and scalable computation.
neurips-2023-gloptinets-scalable-non-con.tldr: GloptiNets uses Fourier regularity and neural-network optimization techniques to scale certified non-convex optimization for smooth functions.

paragraphs: A node classifier must assign labels to interconnected graph nodes, but its predictions also need a useful indication of reliability. This paper focuses on detecting unfamiliar, out-of-distribution nodes and identifying incorrect classifications. These tasks depend on uncertainty estimates that distinguish questionable predictions from trustworthy ones, beyond simply producing a class label.

The authors begin with graph posterior networks trained using uncertainty cross-entropy. They analyze theoretical limitations of this widely used loss and introduce a distance-based regularizer to alleviate the identified problems. The regularizer encourages out-of-distribution nodes that form clusters to remain grouped in the learned latent representation. It therefore constrains the geometry of the representation used for uncertainty estimation.

Experiments on eight standard datasets show that the proposed regularization outperforms state-of-the-art methods for both out-of-distribution detection and misclassification detection. The contribution connects a theoretical critique of the training objective with a targeted change to representation learning. The reported gains indicate that preserving relevant clustering structure can help the studied graph models produce more useful reliability signals.
neurips-2023-improvements-on-uncertainty.tldr: Distance-based regularization improves graph-node uncertainty estimates by encouraging clustered out-of-distribution nodes to stay clustered in latent space.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained on semantically related data can develop similar internal representations, even when the resemblance is hidden by how those representations are arranged. This paper studies how to translate between such latent spaces. The authors show that simpler transformations than previously expected can connect representations produced by different pretrained networks.

Their method directly estimates a transformation between two latent spaces using standard algebraic procedures with closed-form solutions. This allows an encoder from one network to be connected to a decoder from another without additional training. The transformation acts as the connecting component, making the output representation of one module usable by the other.

The authors validate the approach across different training runs, domains, and architectures, including ResNet, CNN, and ViT models, as well as classification and reconstruction tasks. They also demonstrate zero-shot connections between text encoders and vision decoders, and in the reverse direction, with good reported classification performance. These results support the practical usefulness of semantic alignment for reusing pretrained components across otherwise separate models.
neurips-2023-latent-space-translation-vi.tldr: Closed-form transformations align pretrained latent spaces, enabling encoder–decoder combinations without additional training, including across text and vision.

paragraphs: LIMA investigates how much a language model's useful behavior comes from pretraining and how much must be supplied through later alignment. The authors fine-tune a 65-billion-parameter LLaMa model using only 1,000 carefully selected prompts and responses. Training uses a standard supervised loss, without reinforcement learning or a model of human preferences.

The resulting model learns particular response formats from a small number of examples and handles complex requests such as itinerary planning and alternate-history questions. It also tends to generalize to tasks absent from its fine-tuning data. These observations suggest that a small curated collection can guide how a pretrained model expresses capabilities it already possesses.

In a controlled human study, LIMA responses are judged equivalent to or preferred over GPT-4 responses in 43% of cases, with corresponding figures of 58% against Bard and 65% against DaVinci003. These figures combine ties and preferences. The authors interpret the overall evidence as strongly suggesting that pretraining supplies almost all model knowledge and limited instruction tuning can teach high-quality output.
neurips-2023-lima-less-is-more-for-align.tldr: LIMA shows strong instruction-following after supervised fine-tuning on 1,000 curated examples, suggesting much of its capability comes from pretraining.

paragraphs: Decisions made by a machine learning system can change the population on which future decisions are made. This paper treats fairness as a problem of controlling that evolving interaction. It formulates long-term fairness through online reinforcement learning, allowing objectives such as reaching equitable population states that static fairness formulations cannot express.

The proposed algorithm adapts ideas from online learning to a setting where population dynamics are initially unknown. The authors show that algorithmic solutions can learn those dynamics and move the policy-population system toward more desirable equilibria, potentially by giving up short-term incentives. They prove simultaneous probabilistic bounds on cumulative loss and cumulative fairness violations in their proposed setting.

Experiments examine classification with group fairness, using population models based on evolutionary game theory and incorporating real-world datasets. Comparisons include repeatedly retrained myopic classifiers, distributionally robust classifiers, and a deep reinforcement learning method without fairness guarantees. The contribution is a formulation and algorithm that make evolving population outcomes part of the learning objective while supplying cumulative guarantees.
neurips-2023-long-term-fairness-with-unk.tldr: An online reinforcement learning formulation pursues long-term population fairness under unknown dynamics with probabilistic bounds on cumulative loss and fairness violations.

paragraphs: CLIP can recognize visual concepts without task-specific examples, but adapting it to a few labeled examples often involves offline parameter fine-tuning. That process can increase inference time and risk overfitting in some domains. Meta-Adapter instead introduces a lightweight residual-style component that refines CLIP features online using the available examples as guidance.

The adapter is designed to support few-shot recognition and transfer to unseen data or tasks without additional fine-tuning. Its role is to adjust the features used for recognition through a small, reusable module. This makes the method relevant when new examples need to inform predictions efficiently, without carrying out another parameter-tuning process for the new setting.

Across eight image classification datasets, the authors report an average 3.6% improvement over the state-of-the-art online few-shot method, together with faster inference. They also apply the module to open-vocabulary object detection and segmentation and report improvements without further fine-tuning. These findings support both the efficiency of the adaptation mechanism and its usefulness beyond image classification.
neurips-2023-meta-adapter-an-online-few-.tldr: Meta-Adapter refines CLIP features online from a few examples, improving recognition speed and performance while transferring without further fine-tuning.

paragraphs: A molecular representation needs to capture both which atoms are bonded and how those atoms are arranged in space. This paper identifies geometric representation as a bottleneck for applying machine learning to drug discovery. Molecule Joint Auto-Encoding, or MoleculeJAE, is a pretraining method designed to learn from both forms of molecular information together.

The method combines two-dimensional bond topology with three-dimensional conformation. It uses a diffusion process to model augmented trajectories of these two modalities and learns from those trajectories in a self-supervised manner. The aim is to capture inherent chemical structure in a representation that can subsequently support tasks where molecular geometry matters.

The authors evaluate MoleculeJAE against 12 competitive baselines across 20 tasks and report state-of-the-art performance on 15. This provides empirical support for the proposed joint pretraining approach across the tested tasks. The broader motivation is to make molecular features more informative by learning connectivity and spatial arrangement together, with the expectation that the resulting representation benefits downstream geometry-related prediction.
neurips-2023-molecule-joint-auto-encodin.tldr: MoleculeJAE jointly pretrains on molecular bonds and three-dimensional conformations through diffusion trajectories, achieving state-of-the-art results on 15 of 20 tasks.

paragraphs: This paper compares quantum learning when measurements can act jointly across copies, separately on copies, or through quantum statistical queries. For learning a function from the specified quantum examples, it proves that any method using T copies with entangled measurements can be matched using O(nT²) copies with separable measurements. However, learning only a property of a function can exhibit an exponential advantage for entangled measurements.

The authors also construct a class based on degree-two functions with an exponential separation between quantum statistical-query learning and learning with entangled measurements, even with noise. This distinguishes restrictions on measurement access from the amount of data available: different access models can have substantially different learning power.

A new quantum statistical query dimension supplies lower bounds for tasks including purity testing and learning several families of quantum states. Further applications give an unconditional separation between weak and strong error mitigation and lower bounds for learning distributions in the statistical-query model. These results remove a diagonal-measurement assumption used in earlier analogous results.
neurips-2023-on-the-role-of-entanglement.tldr: The paper establishes task-dependent separations between quantum measurement models and introduces a dimension that yields quantum statistical-query lower bounds.

paragraphs: Spatiotemporal graph networks forecast many related time series with one shared model, using graph connections to exchange information. Sharing can improve computational and data efficiency compared with fitting a separate model for every series. However, one global model can be restrictive when some nodes follow different underlying processes and require their own forecasting behavior.

This paper examines how shared and local components should work together. It develops a framework for understanding trainable node embeddings as a way to distribute the learning of specialized components across the model. These embeddings combine shared message-passing layers with node-specific parameters, allowing common relational structure and individual dynamics to contribute to predictions.

The framework also uses embeddings to support efficient transfer of a learned model to new node sets. Backed by empirical evidence, the authors provide guidance for adapting graph-based predictors to the dynamics of individual time series. Their central finding is that this specialization plays a crucial role in forecasting accuracy, making node embeddings a functional part of managing differences between series.
neurips-2023-taming-local-effects-in-gra.tldr: The paper explains how trainable node embeddings combine shared graph forecasting with node-specific dynamics and support transfer to new node sets.

paragraphs: Multi-marginal optimal transport seeks a joint distribution that connects several prescribed distributions while minimizing a cost. This paper studies an entropy-regularized version in which the cost follows a tree structure. Specifically, the total quadratic cost is assembled from pairwise costs along the tree's edges, providing an organized way to connect multiple distributions.

The authors develop Tree-based Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge, or TreeDSB, by extending the Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge algorithm to this setting. They describe it as a dynamic, continuous-state counterpart of the multi-marginal Sinkhorn algorithm. The method uses the tree structure to address a transport problem involving several marginals within one framework.

A notable application is calculating Wasserstein barycenters, which summarize distributions through transport geometry. This problem can be represented by a star-shaped tree, placing it within the proposed formulation. Demonstrations include high-dimensional image interpolation and Bayesian fusion. These applications show that the framework can be used beyond low-dimensional transport examples while retaining the specific tree-structured cost formulation.
neurips-2023-tree-based-diffusion-schrod.tldr: TreeDSB extends diffusion Schrödinger bridges to tree-structured multi-marginal transport, with applications to Wasserstein barycenters, image interpolation, and Bayesian fusion.

paragraphs: TreeVAE combines hierarchical clustering with a generative model. It learns a tree-shaped distribution over latent variables, dividing samples according to their characteristics while representing relationships between the resulting groups. The architecture adapts as it learns, seeking a tree suited to encoding dependencies among those hidden variables and revealing structure within the data.

The tree's leaves have specialized decoders, allowing different discovered groups to use different mechanisms for generating samples. The authors report that this structure improves generative performance and enables lightweight conditional inference. Because the clusters belong to a generative model, users can also condition on a discovered cluster to produce new samples associated with it.

Across several datasets, including real-world imaging data, TreeVAE uncovers clusters and meaningful hierarchical relationships between groups. The paper also reports a more competitive lower bound on log likelihood than sequential counterparts. Together, these findings support using a learned branching structure to organize data and generate it, with the hierarchy serving both as a description of discovered groups and as part of the model's computation.
neurips-2023-tree-variational-autoencode.tldr: TreeVAE learns an adaptive latent hierarchy that discovers related clusters and generates samples through specialized leaf decoders.

paragraphs: Random initialization, subsampling, and shuffling make a learning algorithm's output a mixture of distributions. Accounting for this randomness in differential privacy proofs can be difficult. This paper uses f-differential privacy, which expresses guarantees through trade-off functions, to improve analysis of shuffling mechanisms and a single iteration of differentially private gradient descent with random initialization.

For shuffling, the authors derive a closed-form trade-off function that improves on the latest bounds expressed through epsilon-delta differential privacy considered in the paper. For one-step gradient descent, numerical calculations indicate that random initialization can improve privacy. That finding concerns the analyzed one-iteration setting and is presented as evidence of a possible privacy benefit.

The analysis introduces an inequality for trade-off functions that also implies joint convexity of F-divergences. The authors further develop an f-DP counterpart of advanced joint convexity for the hockey-stick divergence and apply it to mixture mechanisms. These mathematical tools provide a common route for accounting more precisely for randomness when analyzing privacy guarantees.
neurips-2023-unified-enhancement-of-priv.tldr: New f-differential privacy tools sharpen shuffling bounds and numerically indicate a privacy benefit from random initialization in one-step private gradient descent.

paragraphs: Developing automated Parkinson's disease analysis requires a shared way to compare methods. This paper introduces YouTubePD to address the lack of a unified public benchmark. The collection uses existing YouTube videos featuring Parkinson's disease and brings together video, audio, and facial landmarks across more than 200 subject videos, with dense and varied annotations from a clinical expert.

The benchmark defines three complementary tasks spanning discriminative and generative uses, accompanied by corresponding baselines. Combining several information types allows researchers to evaluate methods using more than one aspect of the recorded material. The shared tasks and baselines provide a common starting point for comparing approaches and developing new models.

Experiments show potential for modern deep learning and computer vision methods, particularly their ability to generalize from YouTubePD to real-world clinical settings, while also exposing limitations. The stated contribution is an evaluation resource and evidence about model capabilities. Its relevance lies in making Parkinson's disease analysis more systematically comparable and supporting further research using multimodal recordings collected outside controlled settings.
neurips-2023-youtubepd-a-multimodal-benc.tldr: YouTubePD provides expert-annotated video, audio, and facial landmarks with three benchmark tasks for evaluating Parkinson's disease analysis.
